title: Cap. III Rat.: God rejects only from foresight of sin — so elects from foresight of works
latin: Deus non rejicit nisi ex praevisione peccati: Nam rejectio sive reprobatio est opus justitiae Divinae, quod semper supponit hominem peccato inquinatum. Non igitur eligit nisi ex praescientia bonorum operum; quoniam qui non est rejectus, hoc ipso est electus.
pass_a: God does not reject except from foresight of sin: For rejection or reprobation is a work of the divine justice, which always presupposes a human being stained with sin. He does not therefore elect except from foresight of good works; since he who is not rejected, by that very fact is elected.
pass_b: God rejects only from foresight of sin — for rejection or reprobation is a work of divine justice, which always presupposes a person stained with sin. Therefore he elects only from foresight of good works, since whoever is not rejected is by that very fact elected.

lemmas.lemma: non rejicit nisi ex praevisione peccati
lemmas.gloss: rejects only from foresight of sin
reprobation as work of divine justice

title: Cap. III Sol.: two acts of reprobation — praeterition vs praedamnation
latin: Sol. Revocandum est in memoriam, quod de duplici actu reprobationis in Prolegomenis dictum fuit; nimirum, Reprobationem duos hosce actus involvere: unum negativum, quem appellare licet Praeteritionem sive non-electionem; alterum affirmativum, quem vocare possumus praedamnationem, sive Deputationem ad poenam: Respondeo igitur, si per reprobationem prior ille actus intelligatur, quamvis supponamus peccatum in subjecto reprobato, tamen non debemus cogitare Deum ex intuitu peccati hujus decrevisse apud se non eligere aut non liberare hanc personam singularem. Nam idem peccatum in illis etiam intuitus est, quos voluit eligere et liberare.
pass_a: Solution. It must be called back to memory what was said in the Prolegomena concerning the twofold act of reprobation; namely, that Reprobation involves these two acts: one negative, which it is permitted to call Passing-by or non-election; the other affirmative, which we can call praedamnation, or Deputing to punishment: I answer therefore, if by reprobation that prior act is understood, although we suppose sin in the reprobated subject, yet we ought not to think that God from the intuition of this sin decreed with himself not to elect or not to free this singular person. For the same sin was also looked upon in those whom he willed to elect and free.
pass_b: Sol. Recall what the Prolegomena said of reprobation's twofold act: a negative act — Passing-by or non-election — and an affirmative — praedamnation, or deputing to punishment. If reprobation means that prior act, we may grant sin in the reprobated subject, yet we must not think God from intuition of that sin decreed not to elect or not to free this particular person. He looked on the same sin in those he willed to elect and free.

title: Cap. III Sol.: praedamnation rests on sin foresight; election and damnation not parallel
latin: Verum si per reprobationem intelligatur actus praedamnandi, sive deputandi ad interitum, lubens agnosco hunc actum Divinum inniti praescientiae peccati humani. Sed tum dico non esse paris rationis electionem ad gloriam, et deputationem ad poenam: Nam Deus potest immerentem destinare ad gloriam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, quia bonus est, sed non potest immerentem destinare ad poenam absque intuitu peccati, quia justus est. Observavit hoc discrimen Augustinus advers. Julian. lib. 3. cap. 18. Bonus est Deus, justus est Deus: potest sine bonis meritis liberare, quia bonus est; non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est.
pass_a: But if by reprobation the act of praedamning, or of deputing to destruction, is understood, I gladly acknowledge that this divine act rests on foresight of human sin. But then I say that election to glory and deputation to punishment are not of equal reason: For God can destine the undeserving to glory from the mere good pleasure of his will, because he is good, but he cannot destine the undeserving to punishment without intuition of sin, because he is just. Augustine observed this distinction against Julian book 3 chapter 18. God is good, God is just: he can free without good merits, because he is good; he cannot damn without evil merits, because he is just.
pass_b: But if reprobation means praedamning — deputing to destruction — I gladly grant that divine act rests on foresight of human sin. Election to glory and deputation to punishment are not on equal footing: God can destine the undeserving to glory from mere good pleasure, because he is good; he cannot destine the undeserving to punishment without intuition of sin, because he is just. Augustine marked that difference (Contra Jul. 3.18): God is good, God is just — he can free without good merits because he is good; he cannot damn without evil merits because he is just.

title: Cap. III Sol.: two guilty subjects — damning from crime does not prove electing from virtue
latin: Illustremus hoc quod dictum est hujusmodi exemplo: Sumamus duos homines latrocinii, aut proditionis in Principem suum reos: Utrumque igitur ut ex aequo nocentem Princeps intuetur: vult tamen unum ex iis morte capitis afficere; vult alterum non modo a supplicio absolvere, sed in famulitium suum adsciscere, et honoribus eximiis cumulare. Hic siquis argutetur, Rex horum unum damnavit ex intuitu sceleris commissi, quia nempe et latro fuit et proditor, ergo alterum elegit ad honores ex intuitu innocentiae sive virtutis, quia scilicet bonus et justus erat; falso et ridicule concluserit. Perinde ergo et illi falluntur, qui ab intuitu peccati in voluntate damnandi arguunt ad intuitum meritorum in voluntate liberandi, et ad gloriam eligendi.
pass_a: Let us illustrate this which has been said by an example of this sort: Let us take two human beings guilty of robbery, or of treason against their Prince: The Prince therefore looks upon each as equally harmful: yet he wills to afflict one of them with capital death; he wills the other not only to absolve from punishment, but to admit into his household, and to heap with outstanding honors. Here if anyone should argue, The King condemned one of these from intuition of the crime committed, because namely he was both robber and traitor, therefore he elected the other to honors from intuition of innocence or virtue, because namely he was good and just; he would conclude falsely and ridiculously. Likewise therefore those also are deceived who from the intuition of sin in the will of damning argue to the intuition of merits in the will of freeing, and of electing to glory.
pass_b: Illustrate it so: take two men guilty of robbery or treason against their prince. The prince sees each as equally harmful — yet he wills to put one to death, and the other not only to free from punishment but to take into his household and heap with high honors. If someone argues The king condemned one from intuition of the crime (robber and traitor), therefore he elected the other to honors from intuition of innocence or virtue — that conclusion is false and ridiculous. So too are they deceived who from intuition of sin in the will to damn argue to intuition of merits in the will to free and elect to glory.

lemmas.lemma: damnare ex scelere / non eligere ex virtute
lemmas.gloss: damning from crime ≠ electing from virtue

lemmas.lemma: falluntur ab intuitu peccati ad merita
lemmas.gloss: false inference from damn-intuition to merit-intuition

title: Cap. III Sol. close: why not pardoned alike — beneplacitum; Augustine profundum; defer De Reprobatione
latin: Porro, et illud adjiciam: Si quaeratur, Cur miser iste sententiam mortis subiit? recte respondetur, Quia latro et proditor erat. At si quaeratur, Cur noluit Rex perinde illi ignoscere atque alteri qui in eadem causa fuit? cur non iisdem honoribus afficere? Hic non possumus nisi inepte respondere, Quia latrocinii et laesae majestatis reus erat; sic enim et ille alter quem cogitatione informavimus. Sed respondendum est, Quia visum est Regi pro suo beneplacito alterius misereri, alterius non misereri. Hujus autem discriminis ratio latet in scrinio Regii pectoris, non fundatur in personarum diversis meritis. Obsigno hanc responsionem illo Augustini dicto, Cur istum potius quam illum liberet, an non liberet, scrutetur, qui potest, judiciorum ejus tam magnum profundum, veruntamen caveat praecipitium; Epist. 190. Sed cum ad alteram thesin nostram, De Reprobatione, ventum fuerit, haec explicabimus magis enucleate.
pass_a: Further, I will also add this: If it be asked, Why did this wretched one undergo the sentence of death? it is rightly answered, Because he was a robber and a traitor. But if it be asked, Why did the King not will to pardon him alike as the other who was in the same case? why not to affect him with the same honors? Here we cannot answer except ineptly, Because he was guilty of robbery and of injured majesty; for so also was that other whom we have formed in thought. But it must be answered, Because it seemed good to the King for his good pleasure to have mercy on the one, not to have mercy on the other. But the reason of this discrimination lies hidden in the casket of the Royal breast, it is not founded in the diverse merits of the persons. I seal this answer with that saying of Augustine, Why he frees this one rather than that, or does not free, let him scrutinize, who can, so great a depth of his judgments, yet let him beware the precipice; Epistle 190. But when we shall have come to our other thesis, On Reprobation, we will explain these things more clearly.
pass_b: Add this: ask why the wretched man suffered death — rightly, Because he was robber and traitor. Ask why the king would not pardon him as he did the other in the same case, or heap the same honors on him — here to answer Because he was guilty of robbery and treason is inept (so was the other we imagined). The answer is: it seemed good to the king, of his good pleasure, to pity the one and not the other. The reason of that discrimination lies in the king's breast, not in diverse merits. I seal it with Augustine (Epist. 190): why he frees this one rather than that, or does not free — let whoever can sound that great depth of his judgments, yet beware the precipice. When we reach our other thesis, On Reprobation, we will unpack this more clearly.

lemmas.gloss: reason hidden, not in diverse merits
